subtitle.text: "I don't get this," Will Jacobs grumbled as he tried to do his fourth-grade science homework.
His mother stepped into the doorway and asked, "Will, are you done with your homework? It's almost time for bed."
"No. I'm still trying to answer these questions.
I just don't understand earthquakes. How can the earth shake?"
"Why don't you take a little break?" Will's mom suggested. "That sometimes helps."
After his mom left, Will set an alarm on his phone.
He had just gotten it for his birthday, and he loved the new gadget.
Will put his head down on the desk and instantly fell asleep.
Soon the alarm went off, making the table vibrate.
Will silenced it, ignoring the message on the phone's screen: "WAKE UP!"
He went back to sleep, only to be woken up again by another vibration.
But this time when Will opened his eyes, he wasn't in his room—he was in a dark, long cave.
And the phone wasn't vibrating—the ground was shaking!
"Whoa," thought Will. "What's going on?"
A voice nearby squeaked, "Alert! Earthquake!"
Will looked around but didn't see anyone. Then he spotted a patch of light on the ground.
He looked closer and saw that it was his phone. The voice came from the device!
Will picked up the phone, mumbling to himself, "This is strange. Phones can't talk!"
"Most phones don't talk, but I am a QT-9000."
He almost dropped it again when the phone replied!
"I can talk and do much more. I'm the smartest phone you'll ever have! You can call me QT."
"Wow!" Will exclaimed. "Can you tell me what's happening? Where am I?"
"My sensors indicate that we are in a cave.
And we just experienced a small earthquake," replied QT.
All of a sudden, the ground started shaking again.
"And this is a big earthquake," QT said as a whole section of the rock wall moved.
Will noticed light coming through a crack in the ceiling.
"I'm getting out of here," he said, stuffing the phone in his pocket. He climbed out to the surface.
Nearby a road had torn in half. Will pulled his phone out and asked, "How can a huge part of the ground move like that?"
A map of the world appeared on QT's screen.
"The surface of the planet, called the crust, is made up of chunks called tectonic plates.
There are 12 large plates and many smaller ones," QT explained.
"The plates float on top of the mantle, a soft layer of rock and other materials.
Underneath the mantle is a layer of liquid metal called the outer core.
And underneath that is the inner core, which is solid metal.
It's very hot at the center of the planet, and the heat escaping from there makes the plates move.
The movement is what causes earthquakes," said QT.
"Oh . . ." Will thought for a moment and then asked, "If the plates are constantly moving, why aren't earthquakes happening all the time?"
"Actually they are! Most are just so small that people don't feel them.
Big earthquakes, like this one, happen when friction stops the edges of the plates from moving for a while.
When they finally break loose, they release all that stored energy, like a spring." QT paused for a second.
"My GPS tells me that we are on the San Andreas Fault, in California."
Will's eyes lit up. "We learned about faults in science class!
A fault is the crack between two plates in the planet's crust!"
Will looked at the road again. "That must be a fault over there."
"Yes, it is. Two plates are sliding past each other here, causing powerful earthquakes.
Faults also often appear by mountains. That's because when two plates come together, their edges can wrinkle and fold to make mountains."
Will scratched his head. "What happens when plates move apart? Do huge holes appear in the ground?"
"No. Right now the places where plates are moving apart are mostly under the ocean.
Down there magma—that's hot, liquid rock—rises from between the plates.
It cools when it touches the cold water, so it hardens and becomes part of the crust," QT explained. "Earthquakes can be very destructive.
If that road over there is destroyed, just imagine what can happen in a city during an earthquake. Actually I'll show you."
"How? We're nowhere near a city," Will pointed out.
"Look at my screen and I'll transport us. I told you I have special skills."
Will gazed down at the screen and saw a street in ruins.
Then everything got dark. A moment later Will found himself in the city!
He was standing in a crowded park.
Will was shocked by the destruction around him.
"I'd better stay here, away from the buildings.
My science teacher said that aftershocks always come after a big earthquake, but we don't know when.
It's dangerous because more parts of the buildings could fall. But where are we?" asked Will.
"This is San Francisco after a magnitude 6.9 earthquake," QT replied.
"The earthquake's epicenter was actually about a hundred kilometers away, but you can see how much power it released."
Will looked confused. "What's an epicenter, and what does magnitude mean?"
"Earthquakes start deep underground. The spot on the surface of the planet above the earthquake is called its epicenter.
Magnitude is the strength of an earthquake.
Each point on the magnitude scale is ten times stronger than the one before, so an 8-point earthquake is ten times stronger than a 7-point.
Can you imagine damage ten times worse than this?"
Will shook his head. "No. This is pretty bad. How do they measure magnitude?
Do they count the buildings that fell or something?"
A jagged line appeared on QT's screen. "People who study earthquakes are called seismologists.
They measure earthquakes with machines called seismographs, which monitor the vibrations in the ground.
Usually the earth doesn't move much, so the waves the seismographs draw are pretty small.
But during an earthquake, the waves get really big.
The size of the waves determines the magnitude."
Suddenly the aftershock came. The ground rumbled and then moved.
Terrified, Will shut his eyes. When the sound passed, he slowly opened his eyes.
To his amazement he was back in his room. His phone was vibrating in his hand; the alarm was going off.
"That was a strange dream . . . ," he muttered, reaching for his pencil.
"But QT sure is cool! And now these homework questions will be a piece of cake!"
"Stop that!" Will tried to protect his goldfish from Tish, the family cat.
"Silly cat! Those fish aren't a snack, and I have to study!"
He turned back to his science textbook and yawned.
"This is boring," he murmured, pushing away his homework.
"Isn't the ocean just water anyway? I'm so tired . . ."
Will glanced at the time on his phone, set an alarm for ten minutes later, and crawled into bed.
He immediately fell asleep and started to dream.
Will found himself inside a submarine, floating in the middle of nowhere.
"Wow! Where am I, QT?" he said, picking up his phone.
"My GPS indicates that we're floating in the western Pacific Ocean," QT responded. "See?"
"Wow. That's a lot of water," Will commented.
"Almost three quarters of Earth is covered by water: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic, and Southern oceans.
But they're connected into one world ocean because water moves all around," QT explained.
Will peered at the map on QT's screen. "The continents seem so small."
"They're bigger than they look," QT said. "Wait a second, and I'll take control of the ship."
A beam of light shot from QT to the submarine's controls, and the ship began moving.
"You can do that? Wow!" Will exclaimed.
"I sure can. Right now we're over a strip around the continents called the continental shelf.
It can extend four hundred kilometers from the coast.
But it's not steep, so the water is usually 140 meters at its deepest."
"Colorful tropical reefs and lots of animals live in this area," Will said, remembering something he had read in his textbook.
"That's right," QT said. "Then the ground gets steeper. We call this section of the continents the continental slope.
It goes all the way to the ocean floor." The submarine descended quickly, startling Will.
"Where are we going?"
"Down!" QT answered. "But I've got to turn on the lights.
Sunlight doesn't penetrate very far into the water.
The top layer of the ocean, the Sunlight Zone, is only two hundred meters deep.
In this zone there's enough light for plants to survive.
The fish and mammals that live here feed on the plants and—"
"Each other?" Will guessed.
"Right. As you go deeper, into the Twilight Zone, it grows dimmer and dimmer—not enough light for plants.
So the creatures that live here usually have huge eyes to help them see.
And they tend to come up to the Sunlight Zone to feed at night, when predators can't see them," QT explained.
"That's where we are now, right? It's pretty dark here."
Then Will noticed something enormous in the distance. "What's that? It's getting closer fast!"
"Uh-oh . . . That's a giant squid. They live here, feeding on fish and smaller squid. It probably thinks we're lunch!"
Just as the giant squid was about to wrap its tentacles around the submarine, QT turned the boat sharply, and they sped away.
"Whew!" said Will.
"As I was saying," QT continued, "by one thousand meters deep, there's no light. That's the start of the Midnight Zone."
Will nodded. "This must be it." Then he spied something surprising. "Lights!"
"Many species have adapted to life without sunlight.
Some create their own light, to attract mates or prey or confuse predators."
QT turned off the lights, and a fish with huge teeth swam by.
It had what looked like a fishing pole coming out of its head, with a light on the top.
"That's weird! What is it?" Will asked.
"An anglerfish. It attracts food with that light."
After the fish swam away, QT flashed the submarine's lights. Thousands of lights flashed back.
Will was amazed. "Wow! That's a lot of anglerfish!"
"And some squid, some shrimplike species, and other creatures. We're approaching the ocean floor now.
The ocean floor starts about four thousand meters below the surface, but it can go as deep as six thousand meters."
QT turned the lights back on, and a vast plain appeared before them. It was dotted with mountains.
"It looks a lot like the land above water; most of it is flat, but there are also mountains and valleys.
Those little mountains are called seamounts. If they become big enough to reach the surface, their name changes to islands."
"Cool!" Will exclaimed. Then he noticed something else.
"What are those tubes, with the black stuff erupting out of them?"
"They're called black smokers," QT said. "They release toxic gases and hot water from underground.
For a long time, people thought nothing could live down here, but they were wrong."
QT shined a bright light near one of the smokers, and they saw fish and crabs swimming among long, white tubes with red tips.
"Those are tubeworms. They actually get their energy from those toxic substances. But let's look behind us too."
As the submarine turned, the ocean floor dropped away.
QT said, "That's the Mariana Trench, a huge valley.
Its deepest part is the Challenger Deep, at 11,000 meters under the surface. But life exists even there. Let's go see."
As they floated over the edge, they heard a creak. Worried, Will asked, "What was that?"
QT ran a safety check of the submarine, and "DANGER!" appeared on the phone's screen.
But QT sounded calm. "Our submarine made that noise.
We are under extreme pressure down here, and the weight of all the water above us is pressing on the boat.
We shouldn't go much deeper. We don't want to get squished and—"
But before QT could finish, the submarine window cracked!
A stream of water shot inside, splashing Will.
He woke with a start and saw the cat jump away from the fishbowl, shaking its wet paw. "Tish! Stay away from that fishbowl!"
Will went to his desk. "Oceans aren't boring. They're awesome!" he thought, quickly filling in a worksheet.
Before long, he crawled back into bed—this time, for the night.
Will was riding back to school from a field trip to a museum.
"The Tyrannosaurus was amazing!" said Bobby, Will's best friend.
"It was scary!" Will said. He looked at a photo he'd taken of the dinosaur skeleton with his phone and then glanced at their homework.
"Do you know the answer to number five? Why did dinosaurs disappear?" he asked Bobby.
"Let's answer these questions before we forget everything . . . or before I fall asleep! Buses make me tired."
Will tried to focus on the worksheet, but soon his eyes were closed and his head was bobbing up and down with every bump in the road.
When Will opened his eyes, he wasn't on the bus anymore.
He was in an aircraft, flying slowly over a strange landscape. QT, his phone, spoke.
"Scientists think the world looked like this in the late Triassic, the period from about 250 to 200 million years ago."
"Huh? When?" Will said.
"This airship is carrying us through time. Scientists talk about Earth's history using a special scale called geologic time.
See that display? It tells us what period of time we're seeing.
Experts think dinosaurs, like those over there, appeared during the Triassic.
But let's travel forward into the next period, when dinosaurs thrived."
QT shined a light at the controls, taking over.
The display changed as the scenery outside shimmered and transformed.
"So is this the Jurassic?" Will asked.
"Yes. It lasted until about 150 million years ago.
Some dinosaurs became gigantic, as you can see.
Let's skip forward into the next period, the Cretaceous.
At the end of the Cretaceous, 70 percent of the species on Earth died, including most dinosaurs."
Will nodded. "We learned that at the museum. But what made them disappear?"
"Well, scientists have some theories, but they can't prove them.
One clue is an unusual layer of rock found all over the world.
It's about 65 million years old and contains a lot of iridium, an element that's usually rare on Earth's surface.
It's normally located deep inside the planet or in space, in some asteroids.
This layer of rock led to two popular theories about what caused the extinction."
QT announced, "Here we are—the end of the Cretaceous, 65 million years ago."
The sky was dark, and they were hovering over a field of volcanoes. "There's so much lava!" Will said.
"We are over India," QT said.
"Some scientists believe these volcanoes contributed to the extinction, because they could have brought iridium to Earth's surface in lava.
The volcanoes might have released enough ash and gases—
which then blew around the whole planet—to create a greenhouse effect, trapping heat in the atmosphere.
A warmer climate would have made it hard for many species to survive."
"Wow," Will whispered, watching a dinosaur flee from the glowing-hot rock.
"But there is another possibility. Let me transport us to another part of the planet," QT said.
The ocean appeared on the phone's screen, and the world went pitch-black.
When it became light again, their aircraft was hovering high over a body of water.
QT continued, "Some scientists think a huge asteroid, about ten kilometers across, hit Earth near Mexico 65 million years ago."
A giant rock flew through the air. Will yelled, "Is that the asteroid?"
"Yes. Scientists are pretty sure it hit Earth, but they can only guess what happened next."
The aircraft shook as the asteroid crashed into Earth.
QT went on, "The asteroid might have created a huge fireball and then tsunamis.
As hot pieces of the asteroid fell back to Earth, they could have started wildfires worldwide.
So at first the temperature of the world would have increased."
The aircraft flew closer to the ground, along the shore.
Will stared at the destruction caused by the asteroid. "How long did this take?"
"No one knows exactly—maybe weeks or months.
After the fires dust from the explosion might have blocked light from reaching Earth's surface.
In the following years, plants, which need light to make food, would have died.
Then plant-eating dinosaurs would have starved and died.
And then the meat-eating dinosaurs would have starved and died too."
"How do we know that?" Will asked.
"We can guess when species lived based on their fossils and what layer of rock we find those fossils in.
The species that went extinct don't appear in rocks formed after 65 million years ago."
Will thought about everything QT had said.
"But scientists aren't sure whether the volcanoes or the asteroid caused the dinosaur extinction?"
"It's possible both contributed. There are other factors and theories too," QT replied.
"For instance, some people think mammals ate so many dinosaur eggs that dinosaurs couldn't survive.
And we're not sure whether dinosaurs died suddenly.
They could have been dying off gradually before the volcanoes or asteroid became a problem.”
QT paused, and the scenery outside began to transform.
"We've jumped forward just a few years. See all those animals?
Many mammals, frogs, crocodiles, and even some species of dinosaurs survived the extinction. But we don't know why."
Will remembered the ferocious-looking Tyrannosaurus at the museum and shuddered.
"Did some dinosaurs survive into modern times?"
"Well, scientists are pretty sure birds evolved from dinosaurs, so technically they are dinosaurs.
And modern crocodiles aren't dinosaurs, but they are very similar to the crocodiles that were alive 65 million years ago," QT said.
Suddenly something rose out of the water. Its jaws snapped shut on the tail of the aircraft!
"No!" Will shut his eyes, expecting the crocodile to pull them underwater.
The aircraft shook and then was still. Will peeked and realized that the bus had jolted to a stop in front of the school.
"Wake up!" Bobby said. "I hope you had a nice nap!"
"I had the strangest dream about dinosaurs. I don't think I'll ever forget the stuff I learned today!" Will said.
Will sat at his desk, staring at a picture in his textbook.
"How can huge holes just appear underground? I don't understand," he thought.
He noticed it was already ten o'clock. "I'm so tired I can't even think anymore!
I'll finish this report tomorrow morning," he decided and climbed into bed. Within minutes he was asleep.
Will woke up shivering. He opened his eyes but saw nothing—just blackness!
It was eerily quiet, except for a constant dripping.
Then QT's screen lit up, and Will realized he wasn't in his room anymore.
"You are in Mammoth Cave, in Kentucky," QT said.
"This is the world's longest cave system. People have explored almost six hundred kilometers of tunnels and caverns so far!"
"I wouldn't want to get lost down here," Will murmured. Then, trying to be brave, he asked, "How are caves formed, anyway?"
"Well, there are many types of caves. I'll show you," QT said and projected an image of a cliff on the cave wall.
"Sea caves are made by waves beating on rock for a very long time, hundreds and thousands of years.
The wind can also carve out caves. You often see these in deserts. There are caves in lava tubes too.
When lava is flowing from a volcano, the top gets cool first and hardens, but the hot lava inside flows right out, leaving a cave behind.
Sometimes caves are even formed in glaciers when water flows through the cracks, making them into big holes."
Will looked at the fantastic formations on the ceiling. "This cave doesn't look like any of those."
"We are in a solution cave, the most common type.
This kind of cave is formed when water trickles through a layer of limestone in the ground to the water table, the level where our groundwater starts."
Will was amazed. "Water made this cave?"
"Well, it had a little help. While water is traveling through soil, it becomes slightly acidic.
Limestone dissolves easily in acid—sort of like sugar in hot tea—
so when water flows through cracks in limestone for thousands of years, it forms these enormous caverns.
When the water table drops, these caves are left empty, or rather, full of air."
"So that's what makes the holes, but what makes these weird rocks?" Will asked.
"I'm getting to that. When the acidic water dissolves limestone, it absorbs the mineral from the stone.
When the water drips from the ceiling of a cavern, it encounters air again and the opposite happens; the mineral dissolved in the water comes out.
Every time a water droplet falls, a little of that mineral stays on the ceiling.
Over time the mineral builds up to form stalactites, these cones hanging from the ceiling.
When the drop hits the floor, a little of the mineral is deposited there too, which builds stalagmites, the cones rising from the floor."
"Stalactites and stalagmites . . . I'll never remember which is which!" Will interrupted.
"Here's a trick to help you keep them straight: stalactites hold tight to the ceiling, and stalagmites might reach the ceiling," QT offered.
"Anyway, they sometimes grow so long that they meet in the middle, forming a column."
"Cool," Will remarked. As he continued down the tunnel, he saw another huge formation. "What's that?"
"It's flowstone. It's really common in caves," QT explained.
"And those thin tubes hanging from the ceiling are called soda straws, for obvious reasons."
Will reached for one, and QT beeped in alarm. "Don't touch the formations! They're very fragile!"
After Will pulled his hand back, QT continued. "They can break, and the oil on our hands interferes with their growth."
"Oh. Okay." Will didn't try to touch anything else as he walked along.
Finally QT said, "Well, we've reached the deepest part of this cave system.
It's also the youngest part. We're over one hundred meters below the surface.
You know you've reached the bottom when you see lots of water. There are many underground rivers and lakes."
"And there's something swimming in the water!" Will exclaimed.
"Believe it or not, certain species spend their entire lives in caves.
Caves are unique because the conditions inside them stay the same all year.
It's always dark, humid, and the temperature doesn't change much.
These species have adapted to help them survive here.
Like many other cave creatures, that species of fish has lived in complete darkness so long that it's gone blind. But it's very sensitive to movement."
"It's completely white too!"
"Most cave species are very pale or white.
Since no animal can see without light, there's no need to spend valuable energy developing color."
Will walked up a steep tunnel branching away from the river.
After a few minutes, he leaned against the wall to rest.
"Ahhh!" Will screamed and jumped away. "Something touched my hand!"
He looked closely and saw a little bug.
"That's just a cave cricket," QT explained. "It's harmless.
Its long limbs and antennae are another adaptation.
They help the cricket find food and avoid predators, since it can't see."
Will continued to climb, and soon a glimmer of light appeared ahead.
He reached the top of the tunnel and crawled inside a huge cave.
"Yikes!" Will froze when he spotted dozens of bats flying near the ceiling.
"Don't be afraid, Will," QT said. "Bats aren't dangerous.
They're quite useful; a single bat can eat three thousand bugs a night!
Because they hunt in darkness—in caves and outside at night—they rely on sound instead of sight to find insects."
A bat flew so close to Will's face that he felt the breeze from its wings.
He closed his eyes and took a deep breath before moving again.
When he opened his eyes, he saw that he was back in his room. A breeze drifted in through the window.
"Whew. I'm glad I don't live in a cave," he said, "but maybe I'll ask Mom if we can visit one."
School was over for the day. Will watched his friends open their umbrellas and head home.
Will had forgotten his umbrella. "It's a good thing Dad can pick me up today.
The weather is terrible!" he thought and sat on a bench in the hallway. "I wonder why."
Will's science class was studying weather, so he started to read the chapter about storms while he waited.
After only a few paragraphs, he fell asleep.
A gust of wind made Will open his eyes. All around him was the wide-open sky!
Glancing down, he realized he was in the basket of a hot air balloon, high above the ground.
Suddenly Will's phone beeped loudly. He pulled QT out of his pocket and said, "Hi! The people down there look like bugs!"
"But they'll get bigger if we start to drop," QT warned.
"Quick, pull the silver handles down to start the burners!"
As soon as Will pulled the handles, huge flames shot out above him.
"I don't want to burn the balloon!" he yelled over the burners' noise, letting go of the handles.
An image of a hot air balloon lit up QT's screen.
"We need the burners to heat the air in the balloon.
Hot air is lighter than the cold air outside the balloon.
That makes the balloon float," QT explained.
"Hot air rising is very powerful. It also creates the weather, you know!"
"Really?" Will asked. "How does it create weather?"
"The sun heats the planet, but some areas get hotter than others.
So the air in the hot regions rises, and cooler air moves in to take its place. We call this air movement wind."
"So that's what makes wind!" Will watched a cloud pass by. "Does hot air make clouds too?"
"Not really. When the sun heats water, some of those particles evaporate.
That means they turn into a gas, called water vapor.
The water vapor rises with the hot air. But the air cools with time.
When it's cold enough, the water vapor condenses, meaning it becomes liquid water again.
But the tiny droplets are so light that they float, forming clouds."
Will pointed to a low, gray cloud in the distance. "That's water?"
"Yes. The cloud looks dark and gray because the water is blocking the sunlight.
That feathery one high above us is actually made of ice crystals, not water, because it's much colder higher up," QT explained.
Gazing at the clouds, Will commented, "I like the ones that look like cotton balls best. Their shapes are always changing."
"That's exactly what makes them dangerous! That harmless-looking, little cloud can quickly become a huge thundercloud, over 12,000 meters tall!
Look to your left, and you'll see what I mean."
Will turned and saw a tall, dark cloud in the distance. "Wow! That's huge."
An image of a cloud appeared on QT's screen.
"Thunderclouds form when there's a lot of warm, humid air.
First a puffy, little cloud appears, like that one.
If the cloud stays warmer than the air around it, it grows taller; warm air keeps moving up and up.
The water droplets combine with other droplets until they get too big and heavy. Then they fall to the ground.
Snow and hail also fall when they get too heavy," QT explained.
"It's raining over there! I hope we don't get wet," Will said. "What makes it snow?"
"Snowflakes form when a cloud's temperature is below freezing, so water vapor turns directly into ice without becoming drops of water first.
The ice crystals give each snowflake a unique shape," QT answered.
"Hail is another kind of precipitation. It forms in thunderclouds.
Water droplets are carried by wind from warmer parts of the cloud into colder parts.
The droplets freeze, and when they fall back through the warm parts of the cloud,
the little balls of ice are covered by a layer of water condensing around them.
If another wind carries the ice up again, that layer will freeze, making the hail bigger.
After many cycles of this, hail can become as big as a baseball!"
"I hope that thundercloud doesn't create such big hail," Will muttered, nervously watching the dark cloud. "It's coming this way!"
"We'd better land. We don't want to be up here if that cloud produces lightning!
Pull on that cord to release some hot air," QT instructed.
Will pulled on the cord, and a vent at the top of the balloon opened. They began to descend slowly.
"What causes lightning?" Will asked.
"Well, when rain starts to fall from a thundercloud, it pulls some air down with it.
The falling air and water rubs against the rising air and water, which creates electric charges.
Lightning allows this energy to flow. The same basic thing happens when you touch a metal doorknob and feel a shock."
Suddenly a lightning bolt escaped from the cloud, and thunder soon followed.
Will tried not to seem scared, asking, "Why do we usually hear thunder after lightning?"
"When lightning strikes, it heats the air around it to thirty thousand degrees Celsius!
That makes the air expand very quickly.
As it expands, it pushes the air around it, which creates a sound wave—thunder.
We see lightning first because light travels much faster than sound."
"I heard that you can measure how far away lightning is by counting the seconds between the lightning and thunder.
If three seconds pass, the lightning struck about a kilometer away," Will said.
"That's right, but we're almost to the ground! Get ready to land!"
Will grabbed the side of the basket and closed his eyes. The basket shook as it touched the ground.
Will opened one eye and saw his dad standing over him, gently shaking his shoulder. "Time to go, sleepyhead," he said.
"I hope it's still storming," Will said as he got up. "Storms are really amazing, Dad!"
Will stared at the blank piece of paper in front of him and sighed.
"Wetlands are useless. I don't want to write a report on them!
I'd rather hang out in the backyard." He grabbed his phone and headed outside.
Will got comfortable in his favorite spot, the hammock.
After a few minutes of rocking back and forth, he dozed off.
Soon an annoying buzzing woke him up. "Stupid mosquitoes," Will grumbled.
"I wish they'd all die." He opened his eyes and saw that he wasn't in the hammock anymore but in a canoe.
And dozens of hungry mosquitoes were circling him.
"Actually if mosquitoes died, many other species would die too—ones you like," QT said.
"Mosquitoes are an important part of the ecosystem."
Will got up and sat on the canoe's bench. "A part of what?"
"An ecosystem is a community of plants and animals and the environment they live in," explained QT.
"Each species within an ecosystem depends on the other species for its survival.
If mosquitoes weren't around, the birds and fish that eat them would disappear.
And then the species that eat those birds and fish would die off too."
"I guess I don't want that . . . ," Will said.
"Each species is part of the ecosystem's food chain.
Food chains show how species are connected. Algae and plants form the bottom of any food chain.
They're called producers because they can make their own food from sunlight.
Creatures that eat other plants and animals are called consumers.
Consumers that only eat plants are called herbivores.
Those that eat both plants and animals are called omnivores.
And those that only eat other animals are carnivores."
Will peered into the water. "I see what you mean.
Those little fish are eating plants. And that bird just ate one of the fish!
And—whoa!—that alligator would have eaten the bird if he were a little quicker!"
"Alligators are at the top of the food chain," QT said. "Very few species can prey on them.
When alligators—and all other creatures—die, decomposers, like bacteria and fungi, break down the dead bodies.
They return the energy and nutrients at the top of the food chain to the bottom
so plants have what they need to grow and start the whole cycle again."
"There are so many animals here! There must be a lot of different food chains," Will guessed.
"You're right. Some plants are eaten by mice, which are eaten by snakes, which are eaten by hawks.
And some plants are eaten by deer, which are then eaten by panthers.
The many connections between all the food chains in an ecosystem make up a food web."
"Did you say 'panthers'?" Will asked in surprise. "Where are we?"
"We are in the Everglades, a huge wetland in southern Florida.
Right now we are in a freshwater marsh, a large part of the Everglades.
Believe it or not, panthers used to be common around here."
QT projected a panther sneaking up on a rabbit.
"Now they're endangered and we're unlikely to see one."
"Maybe we can see better from that tower," Will said, paddling the canoe toward it. "But what exactly is a wetland?"
"It's just what it sounds like: an area that is covered by water for the majority of the time.
Wetlands are pretty shallow, usually no more than a meter deep. There are two main types.
Coastal wetlands—as you can probably guess—are close to a coast.
Fresh water and salty water mix there, so only species that can tolerate water that's a little salty can survive.
Inland wetlands are, well, farther inland. They usually form when rain floods a riverbed or another low, flat area.
Wetlands exist on every continent, except for Antarctica, so there is a huge variety of different habitats.
For instance, wetlands where mostly grasses grow—like this one—are called marshes, and those where trees grow are called swamps."
The canoe reached the shore, and Will got out, stepping onto a path to the tower.
When he reached the viewing platform, he said, "There's so much land! Why don't they do something useful with it?"
"Wetlands are useful!" QT exclaimed. "They have several important jobs. For one they protect us from floods.
When a heavy rainfall comes, wetlands act like a sponge, absorbing the extra water and releasing it slowly."
"I guess that's useful," Will admitted. "What else do wetlands do?"
"They clean water as it passes through, absorbing a lot of nutrients and pollutants.
Let's continue to the coast, and you'll see another benefit of wetlands."
As Will paddled along, the scenery began to change; the marsh became a maze of small islands and trees.
"I've never seen trees growing in water before," commented Will.
"We are in a mangrove swamp," said QT, "another habitat in the Everglades.
It demonstrates another major role of wetlands: many species live here and migrating birds stop here to rest.
Plant roots also keep the soil from being swept away by the flow of water and even make it possible for new land to build up."
Will noticed something big and gray swimming nearby. "What's that?" he asked.
QT scanned the underwater creature and replied, "That is a manatee.
They're harmless herbivores; don't worry. They live close to the shore here in Florida.
Sailors long ago thought these animals were mermaids."
Will stopped paddling to watch the manatee. "It doesn't look like a mermaid to me!"
Soon the gentle rocking of the boat put him to sleep.
When he opened his eyes, he was back in the hammock, still surrounded by mosquitoes.
"I guess mosquitoes aren't totally bad. And wetlands aren't useless after all," he said and ran upstairs to write his report.
Will spun in place, holding a basketball in one hand and a baseball in the other.
"If the basketball is the sun and the baseball is Earth, the baseball should go around the basketball," he told himself.
"But why can't we see the sun all the time?"
Dizzy, he lay down on his bed and stared at his homework.
"All I know is that it gets dark at night—not why!"
Will tried to focus on the worksheet, but he soon dozed off.
When he opened his eyes, he was amazed to see Earth and the moon before him.
"Cool!" he exclaimed, pulling his phone, QT, out of his pocket. "Am I on a spaceship?"
"Yes," QT replied. "Earth is beautiful, isn't it?"
"It sure is. But why can I see only one side of it?" Will asked. "And of the moon too?"
"That's because the sunlight's coming from the left, so it can't shine on the opposite side.
On the side that's lit right now, it is day. On the dark side, it is night.
If you look carefully, you can see the lights of big cities."
"I see them! But when the sun rises, the sides will switch, right?"
"What you call the sun rising is not exactly correct.
We don't experience day and night because the sun moves, but because Earth spins on its axis."
Will was confused. "Its axis? What's that?"
QT explained, "An axis is an imaginary line that goes through Earth's poles. I'll show you."
QT shot a beam of light at the ship's controls, and a screen lit up one wall.
"Earth rotates on its axis, spinning like a top, once every 24 hours.
Although the rotation is too slow for us to see in real time, here's a video of the last 24 hours, sped up," QT said.
"The planet is spinning!" Will observed.
"But to us on Earth, it looks like the sun is rising in the east, moving across the sky, and setting in the west."
"Exactly," QT replied. "The view from Earth is quite different from the view from space.
Watch the moon in this next video, and you'll see what I mean," QT went on.
"The moon's shape appears to change—what we call the phases of the moon—but it actually stays the same.
What changes is how much of it we can see.
Half the moon, the side facing the sun, is always lit.
But because the moon orbits around Earth, we can usually only see part of the lit side."
"Oh . . . ," Will said, watching closely.
After the video finished, he asked, "So where the moon is in its orbit determines how much of it we can see?
That creates the phases of the moon?"
"You've got it," QT answered. "But I want you to see something else.
Take another look at Earth out there. Doesn't it look like it's tipping a little?"
Staring at the planet, Will exclaimed, "Hey! It does."
"Earth is tilted by about 23.5 degrees; that means it's not straight up and down.
If we move farther out, you'll see what I mean," QT said.
As they zoomed through the solar system, Earth got smaller and smaller, and the sun came into view.
Will gasped. "It's enormous! And bright!"
"It sure is. It looks small from Earth because it's very far away, about 150,000,000 kilometers.
So the orbit is a long trip. It takes about 365 days to orbit the sun once—"
"That's a year," Will interrupted.
"Yes, it is. Earth's tilt causes the seasons. I'll show you a diagram," QT said.
The screen lit up, showing Earth's orbit of the sun.
"The planet is always tilted the same way,
so the northern hemisphere is pointed toward the sun for part of the year, and the southern hemisphere for another part."
"The seasons in the northern and southern hemispheres are always opposite?" Will asked.
"Right. The hemisphere that's tilted away from the sun experiences winter, and the one that's tilted toward the sun experiences summer.
Right now it's December—winter in the northern hemisphere, where you live.
See how little direct light it's getting compared to the southern hemisphere?
There it's summer because it's getting a lot of direct light.
When the northern hemisphere is tilted toward the sun, it gets much more sunlight, so it's summer.
For spring and fall, neither hemisphere is tilted toward the sun, so the weather is the same."
Will thought for a moment. "Is that why the days are longer during the summer?
Because the northern hemisphere is tilted toward the sun?"
"Absolutely. That's what causes the 24-hour days in the Arctic.
And the Antarctic doesn't see the sun at all, causing 24-hour nights," QT said.
"But I'd better turn the ship around now.
We don't want to be floating out in space forever, do we?"
"No." Will grinned. "I've got basketball practice tomorrow!"
The spaceship started moving back toward Earth, but as they flew past the sun, the ship swerved.
"What's going on?" Will asked. Red lights on the controls were blinking, and a warning bell was ringing.
"We might have gotten too close to the sun," QT said, sounding worried.
"Its gravity is pulling us in!" The ship was going faster and faster, straight into the sun.
Will covered his eyes with his hands to protect them from the blinding rays.
When he lowered his hands, squinting at the bright light, his dad was standing by the bedroom door with his hand on the light switch.
"Why was the light off?" he asked Will.
"I was just napping," Will replied, crawling out of bed.
"Thanks for waking me up. I have to finish something."
He picked up his homework and quickly answered the questions.
"That wasn't so hard," he thought, putting away the basketball and baseball.
